title: Hindsight Bias
description: After an event occurs, you become convinced you “knew it all along,” even when you didn’t. The outcome colors your memory of what you predicted.
shortDescription: After an event occurs, you become convinced you “knew it all along,” even when you didn’t. The outcome colors your memory of what you predicted.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: After an event occurs, you become convinced you “knew it all along,” even when you didn’t. The outcome colors your memory of what you predicted.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: After a stock crash, everyone says “it was obvious” the market was overvalued. Before the crash, they were buying.
A relationship ends, and friends say “I always thought they were wrong for you.” They never said it before.
After an election upset, pundits explain exactly why it was inevitable. Their pre‑election commentary said the opposite.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Rewriting past opinions to match outcomes.
Using phrases like “I knew that would happen” and genuinely believing it.
Forgetting that you were uncertain or held a different view.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I saw that coming a mile away.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel no surprise at an unexpected event.
You cannot produce pre‑event evidence of your prediction.
You dismiss the actual uncertainty that existed.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The brain reconstructs memories based on current knowledge. Once you know the outcome, it’s cognitively easy to fit it into a plausible narrative, and the memory of your prior ignorance gets overwritten.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
sections.content: Keep a decision journal. Write down your predictions and confidence levels before events unfold. Compare later. This is a debiasing gold standard.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming others are lying when they say “I knew it.” They often truly believe their revised memory.
Using hindsight bias to unfairly criticize past decisions made with limited information.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A CEO launches a product that fails. Board members later say “The warning signs were obvious; we should have stopped it.” Meeting minutes from before launch show unanimous enthusiasm and no mention of those “obvious” signs.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The past always looks predictable once you know the ending. That doesn’t mean it was.
